papers.title_in_file: A survey on the complexity of learning quantum states
papers.version_note: arXiv:2305.20069v1, 31 May 2023, as in the brief's file name; text is the paper its record names.
papers.what_it_is: A survey of rigorous sample and time complexity results for learning quantum states (tomography, physical state classes, alternate learning models, classical functions encoded as states) with 25 open questions.

existing.note: The survey says this in Section 1.1 and again in Sections 3 and 4 (full tomography needs exponentially many copies, quantified in Section 4). It gives no proof in Section 1.1; the quantitative bounds are in Theorem 1.
quotes: Given the generality of this task, the sample complexity of this task is known to be exponential in n.
In the previous section we saw that fully learning arbitrary quantum states could require exponentially many copies of the unknown state.

existing.note: The sentence the stored value rests on covers two models named just before it: a noisy-example (classification noise) model and agnostic learning, both distribution-independent. It does not name plain PAC learning; for PAC the survey says separately that quantum examples are not useful in the distribution independent setting [AdW18b]. The conclusion (equal up to constant factors) holds for the two models the sentence names.
existing.value: The authors state that, in two distribution-independent models, learning with classification noise and agnostic learning, [AdW18b] showed that quantum sample complexity of learning is equal to classical sample complexity of learning up to constant factors. For plain PAC learning the survey separately states that quantum examples are not useful under the distribution independent setting.
quotes: In both these distribution-independent learning models, [AdW18b] showed that quantum sample complexity of learning is equal to classical sample complexity of learning up to constant factors.
setting, we know that quantum examples are not useful for learning [AdW18b]
existing.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to [AdW18b], not tested in the survey.
existing.reader_inference: The text layer garbles the sentence that introduces the noisy-example model, so its name is taken from the later mention of the classification noise model.

assertions.value: The authors state that deep learning techniques work very well in practice but are not well understood from a theoretical standpoint.
quotes: Although these machine learning techniques work very well in practice, they are not well understood from a theoretical standpoint.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' statement without evidence in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors argue that learnability as a complexity-theoretic metric is remarkably powerful and has been revealing fundamentally new properties of physically and computationally relevant quantum states.
quotes: Here we argue that learnability as a complexity-theoretic metric is remarkably powerful and has been revealing fundamentally new properties of physically and computationally relevant quantum states.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' statement without evidence in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors define a general formalism: a learner receives many independent copies of an unknown quantum state guaranteed to be within a class of states known to the learner, extracts information by quantum measurements, and outputs a sufficiently accurate description. The three defining notions are the class of states, the type of measurement and the accuracy metric.
quotes: A learning algorithm (which we often refer to as a learner) receives many independent copies of an unknown quantum state guaranteed to be within a “class” of states (known to the learner).
We stress on the three defining notions in this general framework: the class of states, the type of measurement done by the learner and the metric for accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states its own definition here.

assertions.value: The authors define quantum sample complexity as the number of copies of the unknown state used by the learning algorithm, and quantum time complexity as the total number of gates used by the algorithm.
quotes: quantum sample complexity, defined as the number of copies of the unknown state used by the learning algorithm and quantum time complexity, defined as the total number of gates used by the algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states its own definition here.

assertions.value: The survey covers four categories of learning model with rigorous sample and time guarantees: learning arbitrary quantum states, learning physical quantum states (stabilizer states, the Clifford hierarchy, Gibbs states, matrix product states), learning states in alternate models (PAC, online, shadow tomography), and learning classical functions encoded as states.
quotes: Our survey discusses these learning models that come with rigorous guarantees on the sample and time complexity, as detailed below.
Learning physical quantum states. A natural followup question is, can we learn interesting subclasses of quantum states efficiently?
Learning classical functions encoded as states. Suppose the unknown state ρ encodes a classical function, what is the complexity of learning?
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states its own scope here.

assertions.value: The authors define quantum state tomography (QST) as outputting, from many independent copies of an unknown state, an estimate whose trace-norm distance to the state is at most δ.
quotes: output a ρˆ such that ∥ρˆ−ρ∥tr≤ δ (where ∥·∥tr is the trace norm)
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states its own definition here.

assertions.value: The authors describe a simple QST protocol that estimates all Pauli expectation values and applies linear inversion, with overall sample complexity of order d to the sixth power over δ.
quotes: A simple protocol for QST uses T = O(d6) copies
The overall sample complexity is d2 · O(d4/δ) = O(d6/δ).
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' statement without evidence in the survey.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper states the cost both as order d^6 and as order d^6/delta; the quotes are as printed.

assertions.value: The survey defines Hamiltonian learning from Gibbs states: given copies of the Gibbs state of a local Hamiltonian with unknown coefficients, output coefficients close in ℓ∞ or ℓ2 distance; it assumes each coefficient lies in (−1, 1) and that the interaction graph is known.

We make the natural assumption that µ1, . . . , µm ∈ (−1, 1), which simply says that each local interaction has bounded strength.
Thus, we will assume that the underlying graph is known.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states its own setup here.
